answer:
Priority improvements, ordered by impact:

1) Fix internal inconsistencies that damage credibility. (a) The plan says it 'registered the company' in Milestones but then states it 'has not yet formed a legal entity' - reconcile this. (b) The solution claims payment, refundable deposits and verified university accounts are 'handled in the app,' yet the funding ask allocates $10,000 to build in-app payments, damage protection and verified onboarding. Be explicit about what exists today versus what is planned. (c) The pilot reportedly generated $1,940 in volume with 63 renters at a $31 average order, yet 63 renters implies far more than 63 orders if 44% repeated; clarify the order count and how the numbers reconcile (about 63 orders at $31 is about $1,953, so repeat rentals appear unaccounted for). Also reconcile the claim that students 'wore each piece 1.4 times' with the rental-economics narrative.

2) Rebuild the market sizing bottom-up. 19M students x $100-150 yields $1.9-2.85B, but this treats all clothing spend as capturable and ignores that rentals replace purchases at roughly 70% lower prices. Your own serviceable math is also off: 5% of 6M students x ~$125 is about $37M of purchase spend, not 'over $50M' in transaction volume, and rental revenue would be a fraction of that. Replace with: target users x rentals per year x average order x take rate, yielding realistic platform revenue (your fee, not GMV). Show the revenue ceiling honestly; at about $4.65 per rental and 3-4 rentals per user, revenue per user is roughly $14-19/year, which needs to be confronted.

3) Address unit economics and scale of revenue. Pilot revenue of $291 and a 12-month forecast of about $9,000 fee revenue are small relative to a $25,000 ask. Explain how the business reaches meaningful scale, what the path to a seed-fundable metric looks like, and include a cost breakdown (payment processing fees of about 3% plus fixed fees will consume a large share of a $4.65 fee, damage waiver payouts, insurance, ambassador costs). 'Break-even on direct costs' needs to be shown with actual numbers.

4) Strengthen evidence of demand and supply-side liquidity. Survey results are from 412 respondents at one campus; state sampling method and bias. Report pilot funnel metrics: account-to-rental conversion (63/187, about 34%), listing-to-rental rate (how many of 241 items were actually rented), time to fulfillment, repeat lender behavior, and whether students would actually pay versus borrow free from friends. Distinguish 44% second-rental rate (small base, six weeks) from true retention.

5) Deepen competitive analysis. Name specific competitors (Rent the Runway, Nuuly, Pickle, Depop/Poshmark, campus closets and sorority-owned closets) and compare on price, speed and trust. Take the free alternatives more seriously: informal borrowing and Greek-life shared closets are your biggest competitor because they cost $0. Explain why students will pay a 15% fee plus rental price and why lenders won't bypass the platform after the first match (disintermediation risk, which is never mentioned).

6) Add a risks and trust-and-safety section. Cover damaged, stained or unreturned items, deposit disputes, fraud, hygiene and cleaning norms, sizing disputes, liability for in-person meetups, and who bears loss when a $150 dress is ruined. These are the core operational risks of a P2P rental marketplace and the plan barely touches them.

7) Make the go-to-market and defensibility claims concrete. 'Largely organic' acquisition is asserted, not shown; report how pilot users actually arrived. Explain the plan for solving the cold-start problem on each new campus (minimum supply threshold, seeding with sorority closets and ambassadors) and seasonality, since demand peaks mean idle months and churn. The claim that student-organization relationships are hard to copy needs evidence such as signed partnerships or letters of intent.

8) Tighten the ask and milestones. Tie the $25,000 to measurable outcomes (for example, X campuses live, Y paid rentals per campus, Z% repeat rate, positive contribution margin) and a timeline. Clarify the $2,000 'operating costs' line and the relationship between prize money, the founders' personal funding, and the intended seed round. Also disclose the team's commitment level (all are students; are they full-time on this, and what happens after graduation for the seniors?).

9) Minor writing and structure points: lead with the strongest traction numbers; trim repeated claims of distinctiveness; define terms (serviceable market, protection waiver) once and consistently; add a simple table for the financial forecast and use of funds; and cite sources for the 19M enrollment and 600-institution estimates.
